cards.front: The three products inside a maps app
cards.back: A picture of the world that rarely changes (tiles), a shortest-path search that answers in milliseconds (routing), and a live feed of road speeds (traffic).

cards.front: Location ping load for 5M navigating trips
cards.back: A batch every 5 s is 1M requests a second, about 100 MB/s at peak.

cards.front: Why tile URLs carry the map version
cards.back: Tiles are never updated in place, so they are cached for a year; a new version is a new URL and old tiles age out.
4^z (2^z × 2^z). Zoom 14 is about 268M tiles; the deepest level is about 3/4 of all tiles.
Vector tiles send geometry and render on the phone: one set (~100 GB to z14) serves every style and language. Raster tiles need a full copy per style.
Vector tiles stop around zoom 14-16; beyond that the phone scales the deepest geometry, avoiding billions of tiles at zooms 15-20.
Dijkstra grows a circle in every direction; A* adds a never-overestimating estimate of time left so the search leans toward the goal.
Offline, unimportant nodes are removed and replaced by shortcuts; a query climbs upward from both ends, settling hundreds of nodes in under 1 ms.

cards.front: Why customizable CH or CRP for traffic
cards.back: Plain contraction hierarchies bake weights into shortcuts; customizable variants keep the order fixed and apply new weights in seconds.
A hidden Markov model picks the road sequence that best explains a whole GPS trail, since raw fixes wander 5-20 m and jump between parallel roads.

cards.front: How ETAs blend live and historical speeds
cards.back: Trust live speed for segments reached soon; lean on the historical speed for that hour for segments far ahead, plus a learned correction.

cards.front: When to offer a faster route
cards.back: Only when it saves more than about 5 minutes or 10%, and not again soon after the last offer, so the app doesn't flap.

quiz.q: A jam forms on a motorway. Routing uses plain contraction hierarchies and keeps sending drivers into it. Why?
choices: Plain CH bakes weights into shortcuts, so traffic needs a rebuild; a customizable variant applies new weights in seconds
quiz.why: Customizable CH or CRP separates the order from the weights.

quiz.q: Every minute, the server recomputes routes for all 5M active trips to look for faster options. What is a better design?
choices: Recompute only trips whose remaining route crosses a segment whose speed changed a lot
quiz.why: A segment → active trips index avoids about 83k pointless searches a second.

quiz.q: Traffic speeds on a flyover look wrong because cars on the service road below are being counted. What is missing?
choices: Map matching over the whole trail with a hidden Markov model
quiz.why: Matching whole trails stops cars from teleporting between parallel roads.

quiz.q: A residential side street jams because the app sends everyone onto it. What helps?
choices: Track trips assigned to small roads and spread them across alternatives
quiz.why: Large systems spread load and penalise residential roads.

quiz.q: A quiet road at 3 am has no probe phones. What speed does the ETA use?
choices: The historical speed for that hour and weekday, then the speed limit
quiz.why: Gaps fall back to history, then the limit.

quiz.q: Someone walks a cart full of phones slowly down a road to fake a jam. What defends against it?
choices: Require many independent phones per segment and spot outliers
quiz.why: Many probes from few accounts or one spot are suspicious.

quiz.q: A new map version ships. How do tile caches stay correct without a mass purge?
choices: Each version has new URLs; unchanged tiles are copied forward and stay warm
quiz.why: Immutable, versioned tiles never need purging.
